newsitem.title: USA: SoCalGas rate ruling may affect merger with Enova.
newsitem.headline: SoCalGas rate ruling may affect merger with Enova.

text.p: New performance-based rates for Pacific Enterprises' Southern California Gas Co (SoCalGas) could affect the company's planned $5.2 billion merger with Enova Corp, analysts said Thursday.
Pacific Enterprises said it expects to implement most elements of the rate plan as of January 1.

A spokesman for Enova, parent of San Diego Gas & Electric Co, said Thursday the company was studying the rate decision to determine its impact on Pacific Enterprises and on the new company being formed by the pending merger.
The company's board of directors will hold a previously scheduled meeting on Tuesday, he added.

Pacific Enterprises, in a filing to the Securities and Exchange Commission late Wednesday, said the ratemaking plan will make it difficult for SoCalGas to achieve the level of returns it has seen recently.
But the company said it intends to control costs and investment to meet the new targets.
Terms ordered by the California Public Utilities Commission (CPUC) require SoCalGas to cut annual costs by $160 million and to share excess earnings with ratepayers.
If earnings exceed an authorized rate of return, a portion will be returned to customers. But if earnings fall short, shareholders will absorb the whole loss.
The ruling also sets a productivity benchmark for the utility of 2.1 percent in the first year, rising to 2.5 percent in the fifth year of the rate scheme.
"That is a lot harsher than I had expected," said Michael Heim, an analyst at A.G. Edwards.
The CPUC said in a statement the utility's revenues will be adjusted each each year by subtracting the increasing productivity factor, which gives SoCalGas incentive to "stretch" each year.
Revenues are also adjusted for inflation.
Heim noted SoCalGas has already moved aggressively to cut costs over the last couple of years.
But Donato Eassey, an analyst at Merrill Lynch, noted the planned merger will result in extra cost savings.
"(Pacific Enterprises) has a history of over-earning. The merger will mean even more savings," he said.
But he expressed caution about how the CPUC would take account of those savings.
"I just hope they (CPUC) don't go back to them after the merger and try for some double dipping," Eassey said.
He said the good news in the decision is the sharing mechanism for over-target earnings.
"It is good for shareholders if they stay on course," Easey said.
Heim noted Pacific Enterprises and Enova have a working arrangement for the planned merger, "but that doesn't mean they can't get out of it if they have to."
Eassey said there is always some give and take in merger situations and terms could be re-negotiated if the rate ruling proves onerous.
Under merger plans announced last October, shareholders of Pacific Enterprise would to receive 1.5038 shares of the new company's stock for each of their shares.
Enova shareholders were to receive one share of the new company for each Enova share.
The deal was approved last month by the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, but a decision by the CPUC is not expected until next March.
((--Deena Beasley, Los Angeles bureau + 1 213 955 6761))
